consensus.claim: The Autavia name originated in 1933 as a Heuer dashboard timer for AUTomobiles and AVIAtion, and was reused in 1962 as the first Heuer wrist chronograph to carry a model name.
A rotating bezel — marked variously for minutes, hours, MH, tachymeter, decimal-minutes, or 24-hour GMT — is the defining shared feature of every vintage Autavia chronograph.

The first execution 2446/3646 Autavias (1962–~1965) are distinguished by oversized 'Big Sub' registers and fully lume-filled dauphine hands; survivors are extremely scarce and command the strongest prices among manual-wind Autavias.

The screw-back 2446 case ran through two principal executions (1st with wider bezel and rectangular bezel teeth; 2nd with narrower bezel and diagonal teeth), with a small 'Transitional' case (serials ~82,800–83,100) sitting between them — distinguished by lugs that lack the bevel/chamfer between the top and side surfaces.

The 2nd-execution screw-back 2446 ('Mark 3' / 'Rindt') measures ~38.8–39mm with thin faceted lugs and a 13.5mm-thick case, houses a Valjoux 72, has 100m water resistance, and was offered with three bezel options: 60-minute, 12-hour, and tachymeter.
Around 1968 Heuer replaced the screw-back case with the snap-back 'compressor' 2446C (also 7763C, 7863C), where rising water pressure compresses gaskets to improve sealing — an EPSA design.

The compressor case proved less water-resistant in the long term than the previous screw-back, and clean surviving 2446C examples are correspondingly less common; Heuer later reverted to screw-down constructions.
The 7863C 'Dato' (Valjoux 7732) was the first Autavia to feature a date window, placed at six o'clock on a two-register reverse-panda dial.

In 1969, in partnership with Breitling, Hamilton-Buren and Dubois Dépraz, Heuer launched the Calibre 11 automatic chronograph movement, and the Autavia was redrawn into the larger Reference 1163 case (~42mm wide, ~47mm lug-to-lug, ~15mm thick) to house it; the crown sits at 9 o'clock, indicating no manual winding is required.

The very first 1163 Autavias were marked 'Chronomatic' (rather than 'Autavia') on the dial in 1969; Heuer ceded the Chronomatic name to Breitling shortly after, and these earliest 1163s are now among the rarest and most valuable automatic Autavias.

Swiss F1 driver Jo Siffert was sponsored by Heuer from 1969 and wore a white-dial 1163 with black sub-dials and blue accents on track; collectors call this colour scheme the 'Siffert' Autavia, and it is among the most sought-after automatic Autavias.

Reference 1163 dials were tweaked across production (1969–1972); collectors commonly identify six dial 'Marks', with Mark 5 (Arabic 12/3/6/9 on hour totaliser) and Mark 6 (full 12-Arabic hour totaliser) appearing in 1972.

A small triangle on the underside of the five o'clock lug on a 1163 indicates the upgraded Calibre 11-I movement; the Calibre 12 (and later Calibre 15 with running seconds) followed and were commonly fitted during service.

In 1972 Heuer ran a U.S. promotion with Viceroy cigarettes (Brown & Williamson): a Parnelli Jones ad ran in magazines, and customers could redeem a 10-pack carton tab plus payment of $88 (vs. $200 retail) to receive a black-dial 1163 with tachymeter bezel, red-accented brushed hands, and a full 12-numeral hour register — known as the 'Viceroy' Autavia.

1163s that match the Viceroy specification but lack the 'V' suffix after the reference number between the lugs are termed 'Pre-Viceroy', typically dating 1971–early 1972 and slightly less common than the Viceroy promotional pieces.

Heuer-signed Gay Frères beads-of-rice bracelets, date-stamped on the clasp (e.g. '3 71', '4 71', '3 72'), were the period-correct bracelet for the 1163 and are widely considered among the most comfortable bracelets Heuer used.

After the 1163, automatic Autavias moved to the Reference 11630 (mineral crystal, deeper inner flange) and finally the Reference 11063 (the largest case, into 1985); the line also fielded GMT models in 1163 and 11630 form.

Heuer offered an Autavia GMT in the 2446 screw-back, 2446C compressor, and automatic 1163/11630 cases; the GMT hand is read against a 24-hour red/blue rotating bezel and tracks the hour hand (not independently adjustable).

A short-lived execution of the 1163 GMT used red chronograph sub-register hands; pilot Heinz Rengel reported to Heuer that the red hands disappeared under red cockpit night-lighting, and Heuer subsequently changed back to black sub-register hands.
The Autavia was powered across its life by 14 different movements, including Valjoux 72, 92, 7730/7732/7733/7734/7736/7740/7741, and the Calibre 11/11-I/12/14/15 automatic family.

Heuer also produced Autavia chronographs for military issue, including IDF-marked 73463 examples and three known 73663 watches issued to the Kenyan Air Force with radially-arranged Arabic numerals (the so-called 'Shauntavia').

In 2016 TAG Heuer ran the 'Autavia Cup', a public online vote among 16 vintage Autavia designs; the winner — the 2446 Mark 3 'Rindt' reverse-panda — became the visual basis for the 2017 reissue Autavia, which introduced the in-house Heuer 02 chronograph movement.

In 2019 TAG Heuer extended the Autavia name into three-hand watches (the 'Isograph', initially with a carbon-composite hairspring, later replaced by a standard Calibre 5 Chronometer) — the first non-chronograph Autavia wristwatches.

marks.explanation: Original 1962 dial with oversized 'Big Sub' registers and dauphine hands completely filled with luminous material. Fewer than ~20 first-execution survivors are known. Steel-edged hands with lume inserts appear later in this generation.
marks.name: All-Lume (Mark 1, 2446/3646 1st execution)

marks.explanation: Second screw-back dial with applied metal markers combined with luminous dots; relatively short production run, prized for its design.
marks.name: Mark 2 (mixed marker dial)

marks.explanation: Three-register screw-back with polished steel markers and hands (no full lume on hands), standard-size registers and thinner bezel; worn by 1970 F1 champion Jochen Rindt. Won the 2016 Autavia Cup public vote and became the visual basis for the 2017 Heuer 02 reissue.
marks.name: Mark 3 / 'Rindt' (2446 2nd execution)

marks.explanation: Two-register Mark-3-style Autavia worn by Mario Andretti during his racing career; the 'Andretti' nickname follows the same collector pattern as 'Rindt'.
marks.name: 'Andretti' (two-register 2446)

marks.explanation: A small, scarce sub-population of 2nd-execution 2446Ms whose register numerals use Helvetica-style rounded numerals (with uniform-length hash marks) rather than the standard Eurostile-derived numerals. Estimated 200–300 produced; cause unresolved (deliberate variant, dial-printer sample, or pad-printing oversight).
marks.name: Round-typeface 2446M

marks.explanation: Rare interim case (serials ~82,800–83,100) between 1st and 2nd executions, identifiable by lugs that lack the bevel/chamfer between the top and side surfaces. Seen with both 3rd-execution and 3646 tachy dials.
marks.name: Transitional 2446 screw-back

marks.explanation: Snap-back EPSA compressor case introduced ~1968; bezel attachment redesigned between 1st and 2nd 2446C executions. Two bezel-tooth patterns exist for the 2nd execution (smaller and larger teeth). Pushers changed from smooth to fluted between the two executions.
marks.name: 2446C (compressor)

marks.explanation: Late-1960s Autavia in the 2446C compressor case, powered by Valjoux 7732, with a date window at 6 o'clock — the first date-equipped Autavia. Reverse-panda two-register dial.
marks.name: 7863C 'Dato'

marks.explanation: Earliest 1163 dial variant with 'Chronomatic' printed above the shield and 'Autavia' below. Produced briefly in 1969 before Heuer ceded the Chronomatic name to Breitling; survives in both black-dial MH and white-dial 'Siffert' configurations and is among the rarest automatic Autavias.
marks.name: Chronomatic (1163, 1969)

marks.explanation: White dial, black sub-registers, blue accents — the colour scheme worn by Jo Siffert in 1969–71. Mark 5 dial: Arabic numerals at 12/3/6/9 on the hour totaliser; Mark 6 dial: full 12 Arabic numerals on the hour totaliser. Both released in 1972.
marks.name: Siffert (white dial 1163)

marks.explanation: Black-dial 1163 with tachymeter bezel, brushed steel hands with red triangular tips and red inserts, and a 12-Arabic-numeral hour register. 'V' suffix after '1163' between the lugs. Sold via the 1972 Viceroy cigarettes promotion; one of the highest-production vintage Heuers.
marks.name: Viceroy (1163 V)

marks.explanation: Same dial/hand specification as the Viceroy but without the 'V' suffix between the lugs; typically dates to 1971 or early 1972, prior to and at the very start of the cigarette promotion. Slightly scarcer than the standard Viceroy.
marks.name: Pre-Viceroy (1163)

marks.explanation: Early-1970s automatic Autavia with an orange-accented colour scheme, sharing tonal DNA with the orange hands of the 1960s Super Autavia dash chronograph.
marks.name: 'Orange Boy' (1163)

marks.explanation: Autavia variant with a centre-mounted 24-hour hand and a red/blue 24-hour rotating bezel. Produced in the 2446 screw-back, 2446C compressor, and automatic 1163/11630 cases. The GMT hand tracks the main hour hand and cannot be set independently.
marks.name: GMT (Autavia)

marks.explanation: A small engraved triangle on the underside of the five o'clock lug of a 1163 indicates the upgraded Calibre 11-I movement.
marks.name: Calibre 11-I triangle

model_context: The vintage Heuer Autavia is a motorsport-oriented chronograph line whose name combines AUTomobile and AVIAtion. It began in 1933 as a dashboard timer for racing and aviation, and in 1962 became the first Heuer wrist chronograph to carry a model name. The model line covers manual-wind screw-back chronographs (ref. 2446, 3646), snap-back 'compressor' cases (2446C, 7763C, 7863C), and the larger automatic cases (1163, 11630, 11063) that housed the Calibre 11 and its derivatives — Heuer's contribution to the 1969 automatic-chronograph race. The Autavia's defining feature across every execution is the rotating bezel (minutes, hours, MH, tachymeter, decimal-minutes, or 24-hour GMT), used as a functional timing tool alongside the chronograph. The watch was widely worn by professional racers (Jochen Rindt, Mario Andretti, Jo Siffert, Derek Bell, Gilles Villeneuve, Clay Regazzoni), which together with strong U.S. distribution and the 1972 Viceroy cigarette promotion made the Autavia one of Heuer's flagship products through the 1960s and 1970s. The focus references — 2446 (and its variants/executions) and 1163 (Calibre 11/12 automatic) — anchor the two great eras of the line.

source_contributions.unique_contribution: Comprehensive model-line overview: case timeline (1st/2nd screw-back, 2446C compressor, 1163/11630/11063), six primary cases, ~80+ executions, the 14 movements, and the dating context that makes the rest of the corpus legible.
Detailed teardown of the differences between 1st and 2nd 2446C compressor cases (bezel construction, holding spring, knurling, pushers, case-back engraving) and the 2446C GMT dial variants.
Documents the rarely-seen 'Transitional' Autavia screw-back case (no bevelled lugs, serials ~82,800–83,100) sitting between the 1st and 2nd 2446 executions.

Investigation of the rare round-typeface 2446M sub-register dial (~200–300 estimated), with typographer Björn Altmann explaining Eurostile vs Helvetika-derived numerals and Singer dial printing practice.

First-person buying narrative and detailed wrist/case description of a 2446 2nd-execution 'Rindt', including bezel options (60-min/12-hr/tachy), case proportions (38.8mm, 13.5mm thick, 100m WR), and the V72 inside.
Cross-references catalog/advertising evidence (1966 ad art, 1968 Chronosport catalog) suggesting Heuer used round-numeral 2446M dials intentionally rather than as prototypes.
Story of the discovery in Switzerland of the very Chronomatic Autavia used in Heuer's March 1969 launch publicity images, including the dial 'fingerprints' that identify it.

Mark Moss's serial-number batch analysis tying Viceroy/Pre-Viceroy production to specific 1163 batches (241xxx, 246xxx, 266xxx) and noting some 11630s were used to fulfil late Viceroy orders, sometimes with plexiglass crystals.
Side-by-side identification guide for the four black-dial 1163 variants (Chronomatic, ridged-marker MH, polished-marker MH, Viceroy) with rough value bands.
Walks through the valuation of an early 'Siffert' 1163 with original box, papers, and a rare decimal-minutes bezel — and dissects the on-air drama (e.g. the implausible 'can't open the case' moment).
First-person letter from pilot Heinz Rengel explaining why Heuer dropped the red chronograph sub-register hands on the 1163 GMT — they were invisible under red cockpit lighting.

Specifies Mark 6 dial characteristics (12 Arabic numerals on hour totaliser, polished steel hands with blue lume inserts) and notes the Jerry Seinfeld 'Comedians In Cars Getting Coffee' Siffert connection.
Defines the Mark 5 dial (Arabic at 12/3/6/9 only on hour totaliser) and gives a 1972 production stamp ('3 72') on a Gay Frères beads-of-rice bracelet.
Explains the Viceroy promotion mechanics (Parnelli Jones ad, 10-pack carton tab, $88 vs $200 retail, 7-month run) and the 'Pre-Viceroy' distinction (no V suffix between lugs).
Notes the common practice of service-replacing Calibre 11 movements with the upgraded Calibre 12, and that period buyers sometimes requested non-standard bezels (e.g. MH on a 'Pre-Viceroy').
Documents the 7863C 'Dato' — the first Autavia with a date — and explains the EPSA compressor case principle.

Describes the 2446C Mark II compressor (larger bezel teeth, red sweep seconds, black hand inserts) with V72 inside, and notes the 2446 Mark 3 'Rindt' as the 2017 Autavia Cup winner that became the Heuer 02 reissue.
Covers the Abercrombie & Fitch retailer-signed Autavia dashboard timer and the Heuer–A&F partnership that supplied chronographs to the U.S. recreational-racing market in the 1950s–60s.
Distinguishes the 'plain' Autavia dash timer from the Super Autavia dash chronograph (introduced 1958), and identifies its distinctive blood-orange handset and 'Profectus' case alloy.
Jean-Claude Biver's full remarks at the 2016 Heuer Collectors Summit framing the new Autavia as a 're-inspiration' rather than a re-edition, and announcing the Heuer 02 movement.
Sets up the 16-watch Autavia Cup bracket (12 historical + 4 'Fantasy' panda PhotoShops by Paul Gavin) and the public-vote mechanic by which the reissue was chosen.
Round-by-round results of the Autavia Cup voting, showing collector preference for three-register, panda-style designs and the early Mark 3 'Rindt'.
Frames the introduction of three-hand and GMT Autavia 'watches' (non-chronographs) and the editorial debate over extending the model name beyond chronographs.
Anatomy of the 2019 three-hand Autavia Isograph, including the carbon-composite hairspring and the origin of each design element in earlier Autavia generations.
Documents a unique brass-cased green-dial Autavia donated by TAG Heuer to the 2020 Australian bushfire 'Watch & Act' charity auction.
Community 'scrapbook' of the 2012 50th-birthday celebration, surfacing Kenyan Air Force-issued 'Shauntavias', IDF-issued 73463, gold-plated examples, and Peter Moller's 11-movement Autavia line-up.
Cross-model context placing the Autavia within Heuer's 'Big Three' (Autavia, Carrera, Monaco) and against Seafarer/Mareographe/Solunagraph and Camaro lines.
Tells the story of the never-completed silver-dial 2446C SN project and the wide range in quality of later builds completed from leftover dials.
Adjacent context: a Reference 2446 Autavia screw-back case also housed Abercrombie & Fitch Seafarer chronographs, with one selling at Sotheby's in 2021 for $94,500.
Reports the €200,000 listing for a 1st-execution 2446 (Jeff Stein quoted) and the record context — a McQueen Monaco at ~$800k, and a 2446 at Christie's at $125k in 2016.
Buyer-beware example of a 2nd-execution 2446 with replaced hands, redone lume, and an incorrect crystal — a useful cautionary catalogue of typical Autavia 'tells'.
Adjacent racing-chronograph context — Universal Genève 'Nina Rindt' was nicknamed after Jochen Rindt's wife, anchoring the Autavia's Rindt association in the broader collector vocabulary.

stories.title: Jo Siffert and the white-dial 1163
stories.why: Heuer's 1969 sponsorship of Swiss F1 driver Jo Siffert put the white/blue 1163 on the wrists of TV viewers — the 'Siffert' nickname stuck and remains the most recognised automatic Autavia colour scheme.

stories.title: The 1972 Viceroy cigarette promotion
stories.why: A $88 promotional Autavia (vs. $200 retail) traded via Parnelli Jones magazine ads and a 10-pack carton tab put thousands of 1163s into U.S. hands during the Quartz Crisis — the largest single-model run of any vintage Heuer chronograph, and the reason the 'Viceroy' is the most accessible 1163 today.

stories.title: Jochen Rindt and the 2446 Mark 3
stories.why: The 1970 F1 World Champion (posthumous) wore the 2nd-execution 2446 with the 60-minute bezel and Gay Frères beads-of-rice bracelet; the watch carries his name and won the 2016 Autavia Cup public vote that determined the 2017 reissue.

stories.title: Mario Andretti and the two-register Autavia
stories.why: Andretti — winner of both the Indy 500 and the F1 World Championship — was repeatedly photographed wearing a two-register tachymeter-bezel 2446, anchoring the 'Andretti' nickname.

stories.title: Why the red GMT sub-register hands disappeared
stories.why: Pilot Heinz Rengel told Heuer that under red cockpit night-lighting the red chronograph hands on his 1163 GMT vanished against the dial; Heuer changed back to black sub-register hands and added red-edged main hands for night legibility.

stories.title: Finding the original Chronomatic Autavia from the 1969 launch ads
stories.why: In ~2014 a Swiss collector bought a small box of Heuer parts in La Chaux-de-Fonds and reassembled the very Chronomatic Autavia shown in Heuer's March 1969 press release announcing the automatic chronograph — confirmed by dial 'fingerprints' (Chronomatic typeface, shorter 2/4/8/10 markers, distinctive seconds-hand tail).

stories.title: Jerry Seinfeld and the Siffert on bracelet
stories.why: Jerry Seinfeld wears a Siffert 1163 on its Gay Frères beads-of-rice bracelet across episodes of 'Comedians in Cars Getting Coffee' — a quiet, recurring TV cameo for the model.

stories.title: The Pawn Stars 'Siffert'
stories.why: In 2014 a one-owner early 'Siffert' 1163 with original box, papers, and rare decimal-minutes bezel was sold on the U.S. TV show Pawn Stars for $8,000; OnTheDash estimated real market value at $12,000–$14,000 — a useful public datapoint for the model's value and condition factors.

stories.title: The Kenyan Air Force 'Shauntavias'
stories.why: Three Autavia 73663s issued by the Kenyan Air Force, with radially-arranged Arabic numerals, surfaced via UK collector Shaun Wainstein — a reminder that the Autavia had genuine military issue outside the better-known IDF examples.

stories.title: The Heuer–Abercrombie & Fitch sporting partnership
stories.why: From the 1940s, Heuer supplied chronographs to A&F's Madison Avenue shop — including dashboard Autavia timers — for clients like Hemingway, Earhart and several U.S. Presidents; the same partnership produced the Seafarer line, which later shared cases with Autavia references including the 2446.
